Starting from the Cramér representation, we derive that any stationary functional time series admits a spectral decomposition via the operator-valued Fourier transform. This leads to the definition of the spectral density operator Γ(θ), which governs the covariance structure. The Szegő function h(z) emerges as the analytic square root of this density, enabling construction of prediction-error operators via factorization F = ΦΦ*. The Wold decomposition then splits the process into deterministic and predictable components, aligning with GSE’s need to separate stable team performance from evolving dynamics. These primitives fail under nonstationarity or when the spectral density lacks sufficient regularity, rendering them unsuitable for short-season NFL trajectory modeling due to insufficient sample size and temporal instability.
